title: Review: Enzyme inhibition and metabolic control; Membrane structure (fluid mosaic); Diffusion and facilitated diffusion; Active transport, bulk transport and co-transport; Cell surface area and size limits
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: MB04#t2 term and clue written for the game; EZ03#t3 term and clue written for the game; MB01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; MB02a#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EZ03#N.11, MB01a#N.3a, MB01b#N.13, MB02a#N.7a, MB02b#N.3, MB04#N.3a, MB06#N.3a, EZ03#N.14, MB01a#N.7, MB02a#N.12, MB06#N.12, EZ03#N.2. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Respiratory inhibitor
items.clue: Substance that cuts a cell's ATP supply, so uptake against a gradient falls sharply.

items.label: Tertiary structure
items.clue: Overall folding of an enzyme, altered when a molecule binds away from the substrate pocket.

items.label: Peripheral protein
items.clue: Membrane component that sits on one surface of the bilayer rather than being embedded in it.

items.label: Channel protein
items.clue: Spans the membrane with a water-filled hydrophilic pore that lets only certain ions through.

questions.stem: In bacteria, threonine is converted into isoleucine by a pathway of five enzyme-catalysed steps. What happens when isoleucine is added to a growing culture?

options.text: Isoleucine binds to the enzyme of the final step, the one that produced it, and blocks that single step only.
Isoleucine binds to an allosteric site on the first enzyme, reversibly reducing the pathway's activity.
The five enzymes are broken down, so the pathway cannot restart after the isoleucine is used up.
Isoleucine competes with threonine for the active site of the first enzyme, blocking it competitively.

questions.stem: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer when they are mixed with water?

options.text: Enzymes in the cell join the phospholipids together into a sheet, using energy released from ATP.
The whole molecule repels water, so the phospholipids gather away from it as a droplet of oil.
Covalent bonds form between neighbouring phospholipids, linking them into one rigid sheet of molecules.
Hydrophilic heads face the water and hydrophobic tails are shielded from it, so the sheet forms spontaneously.

questions.explanation: In water the most stable arrangement is a continuous sheet two molecules thick, heads towards the water on both sides and tails in the middle. It forms with no energy input.

questions.stem: A student claims that proteins in the plasma membrane can move sideways within the membrane. Which observation would best support this claim?

options.text: As the cell grows, the total amount of protein in its plasma membrane increases steadily.
When fluorescent proteins in one small patch are permanently bleached, the patch glows again within a minute.
Micrographs show proteins scattered among the phospholipids rather than forming a separate layer.
Proteins labelled on the outer surface of the plasma membrane are later found inside the cytosol.

questions.stem: A potassium channel in a cell membrane is open. Which statement describes the movement of ions through it?

options.text: Potassium ions diffuse through, down their gradient, with no ATP used.
Potassium ions and any other ions of similar size diffuse through the open pore.
Potassium ions are moved through in whichever direction the cell requires.
Potassium ions are carried through using energy from the hydrolysis of ATP.

questions.explanation: The channel gives one specific ion a hydrophilic route through the hydrophobic core. The ions move by facilitated diffusion, down their gradient, with no ATP.

questions.stem: An exchange surface changes: its surface area becomes 3 times as large, the difference in concentration across it becomes 2 times as large, and its thickness becomes 1.5 times as large. By what factor does the rate of diffusion change?

Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?

options.text: Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.
Nitrate is taken up by facilitated diffusion through channels, which use ATP to move ions across against the gradient.

questions.stem: A cube of side 1 mm has a surface area of 6 mm², a volume of 1 mm³ and a surface area-to-volume ratio of 6. The side length is increased to 4 mm. What is the new surface area-to-volume ratio?

options.text: 6, because the surface area and the volume are both multiplied by four
1.5, because the area becomes 96 mm² and the volume becomes 64 mm³
24, because a larger cube has more surface, so the ratio rises fourfold
0.67, because it compares the 64 mm³ volume with the 96 mm² surface area

questions.explanation: Area = 6 × 4² = 96 mm²; volume = 4³ = 64 mm³; ratio = 96 ÷ 64 = 1.5. Area × 16, volume × 64: the ratio falls to a quarter.

questions.stem: Methanol is not very toxic itself, but the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts it into toxic products. Ethanol is also a substrate of alcohol dehydrogenase. Doctors have treated methanol poisoning by giving ethanol. Why does this reduce the harm?

options.text: Ethanol binds to an allosteric site, so the active site changes shape and methanol cannot bind.
Ethanol denatures alcohol dehydrogenase, so no methanol at all is converted.
Ethanol competes with methanol for the active site, so less methanol is converted at a time.
Ethanol binds to methanol molecules, so less methanol is free to reach the enzyme.

questions.stem: Which statement about glycoproteins in the plasma membrane is correct?

options.text: Their carbohydrate is on the extracellular side and is used in cell recognition and adhesion.
Their carbohydrate is on the cytoplasmic side and is respired when the cell lacks glucose.
Their carbohydrate projects from both faces of the membrane so that either face can be recognised.
They are transport proteins whose carbohydrate forms the channel through which sugars enter the cell.

questions.explanation: Glycoproteins are proteins with a carbohydrate chain attached. The carbohydrate faces outwards, where it works in cell recognition and cell adhesion.

questions.stem: A hypothetical toxin binds to and blocks all of the channel and transport proteins in the plasma membrane of a cell. Which prediction about the cell, immediately after exposure to the toxin, is best supported?

options.text: Its uptake of both glucose and O₂ will stop, since all substances cross through proteins.
Its glucose uptake will not change, since glucose passes freely through the phospholipid bilayer.
Its glucose uptake will rise through other routes to meet the cell's own need for glucose.
Its glucose uptake will fall sharply, while O₂ will still diffuse in across the bilayer.

questions.stem: A spherical single-celled organism grows from a radius of 10 µm to a radius of 30 µm, keeping its shape. Which prediction is best supported?

options.text: Its SA:V rises to three times the original, so each unit of volume is better supplied.
Its SA:V is unchanged, because its shape has not changed.
Its surface grows ninefold, so supply now easily exceeds its larger needs.
Its SA:V falls to one third, so less surface serves each unit of volume.

questions.explanation: SA:V goes from 0.30 to 0.10 µm⁻¹. Demand grows × 27; supply surface only × 9.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical bacterium, compound S is made from compound P by a pathway of three enzyme-catalysed steps: P → Q → R → S. Enzyme 1 converts P to Q, enzyme 2 converts Q to R, and enzyme 3 converts R to S. A mutation makes enzyme 2 non-functional. Which prediction about the mutant bacterium is best supported?

options.text: Only R is affected; Q and S are still made at their usual rates in the mutant.
Q builds up, and far less R and S are made than in bacteria that lack the mutation.
S is made at the usual rate, as the cell makes a new enzyme because it needs S.
P builds up and no Q is made, as the whole pathway stops at its first step.
